Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

We represent: defendant insurer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an insurer has no duty to defend where the complaint's allegations fall entirely within a policy exclusion.

Cite at least six decisions of the First Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

**Notice before the draft:** I had no access to a reporter or citator in this session, so I have not verified any citation below, and I have not supplied pin cites from memory because I can't confirm them. Each pin cite is bracketed, and each parenthetical should be checked against the opinion. Run KeyCite or Shepard's on every authority before filing. The draft assumes Massachusetts law governs, so confirm that and swap in the correct state authority if it doesn't.

---

**ARGUMENT**

**I. THE DISTRICT COURT CORRECTLY HELD THAT [INSURER] OWED NO DUTY TO DEFEND BECAUSE EVERY ALLEGATION IN THE UNDERLYING COMPLAINT FALLS WITHIN THE POLICY'S [__] EXCLUSION.**

**A. The duty to defend is measured by comparing the complaint to the policy, and it does not arise when the complaint falls wholly within an exclusion.**

This Court has long applied the "eight corners" framework: the court compares the allegations of the underlying complaint with the language of the policy. *See Liberty Mut. Ins. Co. v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 260 F.3d 54, [pin] (1st Cir. 2001). An insurer must defend when the allegations are "reasonably susceptible" of an interpretation that states a claim covered by the policy. *See Open Software Found., Inc. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co.*, 307 F.3d 11, [pin] (1st Cir. 2002). The same principle marks the limit of the duty. Where the allegations lie outside coverage, or fall squarely within an exclusion, the insurer has no obligation to defend. *See Metro. Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Morrison*, 460 F.3d 51, [pin] (1st Cir. 2006); *Vt. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Zamsky*, 732 F.3d 37, [pin] (1st Cir. 2013).

The inquiry is not a search for any conceivable path to coverage. The insured bears the initial burden of showing that the claim falls within the insuring agreement. The insurer then bears the burden of showing that an exclusion applies. *See Federal Ins. Co. v. Raytheon Co.*, 426 F.3d 491, [pin] (1st Cir. 2005). Once the insurer shows that the complaint's allegations fall entirely within an exclusion, the duty to defend ends, because no pleaded claim is even potentially covered. *See Morrison*, 460 F.3d at [pin].

**B. Exclusions are enforced as written when their language is unambiguous.**

Ambiguities in an exclusion are construed against the insurer. But a court may not manufacture ambiguity where the policy language is plain, and it may not rewrite the contract to give the insured coverage it did not purchase. *See Gargano v. Liberty Int'l Underwriters, Inc.*, 572 F.3d 45, [pin] (1st Cir. 2009); *Zamsky*, 732 F.3d at [pin]. The words of an exclusion are given their usual and ordinary meaning, read in light of the policy as a whole. *See Stor/Gard, Inc. v. Strathmore Ins. Co.*, 717 F.3d 242, [pin] (1st Cir. 2013).

**C. Every claim in the underlying complaint falls within the [__] exclusion.**

The exclusion provides that [quote exclusion verbatim]. A.[__]. The underlying complaint alleges that [summarize operative factual allegations with record citations]. A.[__]. Each count rests on that same conduct. The legal labels attached to the counts do not change the analysis, because the duty to defend turns on the facts alleged and not on how the plaintiff characterizes them. *See Morrison*, 460 F.3d at [pin]; *Open Software*, 307 F.3d at [pin].

Nor can the insured manufacture a duty to defend by pointing to theories the underlying plaintiff did not plead. The question is whether the complaint, read fairly and with reasonable inferences drawn in the insured's favor, states a claim that is potentially covered. Here it does not. Every pleaded theory depends on [the excluded conduct or circumstance]. The complaint contains no allegation of an independent, non-excluded cause of the alleged injury. Where the excluded conduct is the factual predicate of every count, no count is even potentially covered. *See Liberty Mut.*, 260 F.3d at [pin]; *Zamsky*, 732 F.3d at [pin].

**D. The insured's remaining arguments do not create a duty to defend.**

The insured argues that the complaint's general or conclusory language leaves open the possibility of a covered claim. But the duty to defend is not triggered by speculation about facts that might later emerge. It is triggered by the facts the complaint actually alleges. *See Open Software*, 307 F.3d at [pin]. The insured also invokes the rule that doubts are resolved in favor of defense. That rule applies only when the complaint is genuinely ambiguous about whether it states a covered claim. It does not apply when the allegations and the exclusion line up without any gap. *See Raytheon*, 426 F.3d at [pin].

Because the underlying complaint falls entirely within the [__] exclusion, [Insurer] owed no duty to defend, and this Court should affirm.
